newsitem.title: UK: German BETA refinery to hike capacity over 20 pct.
newsitem.headline: German BETA refinery to hike capacity over 20 pct.

text.p: Throughput capacity of crude oil at the BETA refinery at Wilhelmshaven in Germany will be increased by over 20 percent this summer when new heat exchanging equipment is added, said Hans Van Weelden, the managing director of the refinery on Monday.
The investment in more energy efficient heat exchanging equipment will raise crude throughput capacity to 10.3 million tonnes per year from the 8.5 million tonnes processed in 1996.
That means a possible 207,000 barrels per day (bpd) from just over 170,000 bpd last year.

"The cost per barrel to process crude will fall," he said. The new equipment will be installed during routine maintenance at the plant this summer, and will increase the surface area of the heat exchangers.
The total investment will be $30 million or 50 million marks, said Van Weelden.
French trading house Louis Dreyfus finally won complete control of the BETA refinery in Germany last week after a bad tempered spat with the plants former co-owners lasting several years.
Louis Dreyfus paid about $60 million refinery after outbidding Bulk Oil AG last Thursday, said industry sources.
Sources familiar withe companies said Bulk Oil AG, the second bidder, has the same majority shareholders as former co-owners Tusculum Holding BV.
"The sale was decided on Thursday February 20 to Wilhelmshavener Raffineriegesellschaft mbH i.G., which is owned by Dreyfus," van Weelden told Reuters earlier on Monday.
Van Weelden said the sale ended a tussle over the refinery between former co-owners Cie Louis Dreyfus SA and Holding Tusculum BV, which had sent the facility into receivership last May.
Louis Dreyfus had invested over $200 million in recent years in an effort to make the plant competitive but was frustrated by a lack of cash from Tusculum, said oil traders.
The refinery is located at the northern tip of Germany with limited access to consuming markets and has little upgrading equipment by modern standards.

These apparent drawbacks dissuaded many potentially buyers from bidding for the plant which eventually only attracted firm bids from Louis Dreyfus, Bulk Oil AG and a management buy-out consortium led by Van Weelden.
"We just couldn't make the figures work," said a source who dropped out of the bidding last year.

Despite some drawbacks the refinery enjoys some of the lowest operating costs in Europe and has managed to carve out a niche selling low sulphur "green" diesel and semi-finished oil products to other refiners for further upgrading.
